subject: business
title: Playing to Win: strategy as five integrated choices, not a wish list
dek: A.G. Lafley and Roger L. Martin’s 2013 Harvard Business Review Press book (and the September 2012 HBR precursor “Bringing Science to the Art of Strategy”) treat strategy as a cascade: winning aspiration, where to play, how to win, capabilities, management systems. The Olay “masstige” rebuild is the teaching case; Pringles’ warehouse can versus Frito-Lay’s fragile bag is the where-to-play contrast. Cite only what named public pages state.

thumb.alt: Walmart beauty aisle shelves with branded skincare and cosmetics packaging in a Toronto mall store.

hero.alt: A brightly lit Walmart beauty section in Dufferin Mall, Toronto, with rows of skincare and makeup bottles.
hero.caption: Walmart beauty aisle, Dufferin Mall, Toronto, 2023. Mass food/drug/discount shelves are the channel Olay’s “masstige” strategy chose to stay in — convenience without a department-store counter — while raising product, packaging, and price. This photo is the channel type, not a claim that this Toronto endcap ran the 1999 Total Effects launch set.

honesty: This is a strategy-framework lesson, not a P&G company biography and not a guarantee that writing five cascade boxes raises sales. Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works (Harvard Business Review Press, 2013) by A.G. Lafley and Roger L. Martin is the named book; the September 2012 HBR essay “Bringing Science to the Art of Strategy” (Lafley, Martin, Jan W. Rivkin, Nicolaj Siggelkow) is the named magazine precursor. Olay facts in this capsule are taken from Martin’s own public accounts — especially his August 2021 Medium essay “Compelling Communication for Your Strategy” and his February 2013 Motley Fool interview — plus the February 2013 Globe and Mail review and the February 2013 Business Insider interview with Lafley. Where those public pages disagree on a number (for example Martin’s Medium essay names women aged 25–49 for where-to-play while his Motley Fool interview says 35 to 50; Medium says the brand grew to a $2.5 billion powerhouse while the interview says almost $3 billion), both figures are flagged rather than averaged into a fake precision. Price points $18.99 for early Olay Total Effects versus a prior mass-channel top near $4.99 / prior Oil of Olay near $3.99–$4.99 are taken from those same Martin accounts. The Pringles versus Frito-Lay where-to-play contrast is Martin’s illustration in that Medium essay, not a claim that Pringles was designed with the 2013 book vocabulary in 1968. Michael Porter is named where Martin’s Monitor/Porter lineage is discussed in the Globe and Mail review; this lesson does not re-teach Five Forces. Blue Ocean Strategy and Jobs to Be Done from earlier Saturday capsules are named only for overlap and difference. Do not invent P&G internal memos, Exact sales charts not on the cited pages, or retailer co-investment contract terms.

fun_fact.title: The opposite of “care about customers” is not a strategy
fun_fact.text: In his August 2021 Medium essay, Martin says listing things whose opposite is stupid on its face — care about customers, hire good people — muddies strategy communication. Strategy, on his account, is the few distinctive choices that let you win relative to rivals, short enough for one cascade page. A hundred-page deck of non-stupid hygiene is a plan, not a strategy.

sections.title: When “strategy” is a vision, a budget, and a refusal to choose

blocks.text: In a 5 February 2013 Business Insider interview timed to the release of Playing to Win: How Strategy Really Works, A.G. Lafley, then recently known as Procter & Gamble’s highly successful former CEO, named three reasons firms keep mangling strategy. People dislike choices because choices close options and create personal risk. Many managers prefer to believe that better execution alone will win. And large companies often do half the job: a vision statement, some industry slides, an annual plan and budget — “parts of strategy, or they’re the output of strategy but they’re not strategy,” Lafley said.

Roger L. Martin, then dean of the University of Toronto’s Rotman School of Management and Lafley’s long-time strategy adviser, put the same complaint in plain words in a Motley Fool interview three weeks later: a strategy that is only a compilation of what every direct report wants to do is a plan, not a choice about where to win. An aspiration that says “be the best” without a where-to-play and how-to-win is a slogan. The book they published with Harvard Business Review Press in 2013 is their joint answer: demystify strategy into five questions that must fit together, then force the organization to answer them with enough precision that something plausible is left out.

blocks.alt: Formal portrait of A.G. Lafley in a dark suit against a dark background.
blocks.caption: A.G. Lafley, company portrait released under a Creative Commons license by Procter & Gamble. Lafley is co-author of Playing to Win and of the September 2012 HBR essay with Martin. The photo is a portrait of the executive, not a scoreboard of Olay sales.
blocks.credit: Procter & Gamble / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 3.0

blocks.text: Harvey Schachter’s Globe and Mail review the same week traced Martin’s toolkit partly to Michael Porter’s teaching via Martin’s earlier Monitor Consulting work. Porter’s 1996 HBR essay “What Is Strategy?” already insisted that strategy requires trade-offs and fit among activities. Lafley and Martin keep that pressure and give operators a cascade they can draw on one page: aspiration, field, advantage, capabilities, systems.

sections.title: Five choices that constrain each other — or you do not have a strategy

blocks.text: The cascade, as the HBR Press book page and Lafley’s interview both state it, is five questions. What is our winning aspiration? Where will we play? How will we win? What capabilities must we have in place to win? What management systems are required to support our choices? Martin’s later Practitioner Insights essays label the middle pair as an inseparable match: a glamorous where-to-play with no credible how-to-win is wishful; a clever how-to-win aimed at a field you refuse to resource is theater.

Winning aspiration is not a laminated mission about caring. In the Olay case Martin describes publicly, the aspiration was to build one of the world’s leading skin-care brands that could anchor P&G Beauty — not merely to “satisfy users of pink cream.” Where to play forces exclusions: which countries, price bands, channels, and age cohorts you will serve, and which you will not. How to win names the reason those chosen customers would prefer you — product, experience, cost, or a combination that rivals cannot copy cheaply. Capabilities are the few things the firm must become distinctively good at to deliver that how-to-win. Management systems are the budgets, metrics, partnering rules, and talent practices that keep those capabilities alive after the launch meeting ends.

The September 2012 HBR essay “Bringing Science to the Art of Strategy,” by Lafley, Martin, Jan W. Rivkin, and Nicolaj Siggelkow, supplies the method for choosing among cascades. Do not start by arguing from last year’s spreadsheet. Frame a choice, generate genuine possibilities, list what would have to be true for each possibility to work, identify the conditions you doubt most, design tests for those conditions, run the tests, then choose. The scientific move is to test the load-bearing beliefs before you fall in love with a deck. Analysis still matters; it comes after the possibilities are sharp enough to be wrong.

blocks.alt: Roger Martin seated on a World Economic Forum stage set in Davos, January 2013.
blocks.caption: Roger Martin, then dean of the Rotman School of Management, at the World Economic Forum in Davos, 24 January 2013 — the same month Playing to Win was released. Portrait of the co-author, not a cascade chart.
blocks.credit: World Economic Forum / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 2.0

blocks.alt: Exterior of the Rotman School of Management building on the University of Toronto campus.
blocks.caption: Rotman School of Management, University of Toronto. Martin was dean here while advising Lafley and co-writing Playing to Win. The building marks the academic side of the partnership, not a claim that every Rotman class taught the Olay cascade.

blocks.text: Martin’s communication rule, stated in his August 2021 Medium essay, is ruthless on length. If you cannot put the distinctive choices on one cascade page, you probably have a plan of non-stupid activities. Strategy, on this view, is the short list of choices that make you distinctive relative to competitors — including the things you will not do.

sections.title: Olay’s masstige cascade, and a chip can that refused Frito-Lay’s field

people.text: In the Motley Fool interview Martin names her as then running Skin Care in the nested choice stack under Beauty — an illustration that cascade choices repeat at every level, not a full biography.

blocks.text: Oil of Olay in the late 1990s is the stuck brand in Martin’s public tellings. His August 2021 Medium essay describes a slowly growing brand around $750 million, ranked outside the top five skin-care brands. The Motley Fool interview adds “no-growth, not very high margin,” and a shelf price he remembers as $3.99. The industry’s habitual where-to-play, in that interview, was women 50 and older focused on wrinkles. P&G needed a skin-care brand that could make Beauty credible; buying a hot rival or launching a clean new name were options on the table, the Globe and Mail review notes. The choice they documented later was to rebuild Olay.

blocks.alt: 1952 Oil of Olay bottle and carton from P&G heritage materials.
blocks.caption: 1952 Oil of Olay package, from Procter & Gamble Heritage Center materials on Commons. The heritage bottle stands for the long mass-cream identity the late-1990s team had to move past — not for the $18.99 Total Effects SKU.
blocks.credit: Procter and Gamble Heritage Center / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: Where to play, in Martin’s Medium cascade, targeted women aged 25–49 noticing first signs of aging rather than the 50-plus cohort the industry overcrowded. (In the Motley Fool interview he says 35 to 50 — same direction, different band; this lesson does not invent a third number.) The channel choice was to stay in mass food, drug, and discount stores — Walmart, CVS, Kroger, and peers in his examples — not to enter prestige department and specialty doors as the primary bet. How to win was “masstige”: combine mass-channel convenience and the absence of pushy counters with prestige-like product quality, packaging, and information. The price tell in his accounts is sharp. Early Olay Total Effects listed at $18.99 when prior mass skin-care tops sat near $4.99 (Medium) or when Oil of Olay itself had been about $3.99 (interview). The marketing promise named in the interview and the Globe review was to fight the “seven signs of aging” with better actives — not merely to pinken the old jar.

blocks.alt: Wide view of a Walmart health and beauty aisle with densely packed personal-care shelves.
blocks.caption: Health and beauty aisle, Walmart Vegreville, Alberta, 2021. Martin’s how-to-win for Olay required mass retailers to host a more prestige-like shelf experience — fuller, better packaged, more informative — which in his Medium essay meant new co-investment and trade-spending systems, not only a formula change.

blocks.text: Capabilities and systems followed the pair. Martin’s Medium essay lists stronger skin-care R&D and outside-lab connections, retailer partnerships to build in-store environments, and beauty-influencer / magazine-editor work unusual for a classic mass brand. Management systems had to allow higher trade spending and co-investment than P&G’s older mass routines assumed. The Globe and Mail review adds Ideo and Saatchi & Saatchi as named partners in the public retelling of packaging and communication work. Outcome claims in Martin’s own mouth: Medium says Olay became the number-one skin-care brand in the world in the 2000s and a $2.5 billion powerhouse; the Motley Fool interview says almost $3 billion and more than 10 percent annual growth for a decade. Both are his public figures; neither is independently re-audited in this capsule.

blocks.alt: 1975 Oil of Olay and Olay Night Cream bottles and cartons.
blocks.caption: 1975 Oil of Olay and Olay Night Cream, P&G Heritage Center. A mid-century mass face of the brand — useful as “before” packaging culture, not as a barcode for Total Effects.
blocks.credit: Procter and Gamble Heritage Center / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY-SA 4.0

blocks.text: Pringles is Martin’s cleaner where-to-play diagram in the same Medium essay. Frito-Lay’s field was whole chips in fragile bags moved by expensive direct store delivery. Pringles, launched by P&G in 1968, was engineered as a reconstituted chip stacked in a robust can that could ride ordinary warehouse distribution. Overlap with Frito-Lay’s system was deliberately small, so the two could coexist for decades. Martin contrasts that with Citrus Hill orange juice in the 1980s, where P&G parked a where-to-play directly on top of Minute Maid’s frozen concentrate and fought a scale war it eventually exited. The lesson inside Playing to Win’s toolkit: if your where-to-play sits on a rival’s exact field, your how-to-win must be extraordinarily strong; separation is often the cheaper strategy.

blocks.alt: Tall Procter & Gamble world headquarters towers in Cincinnati under a blue sky.
blocks.caption: Procter & Gamble world headquarters, Cincinnati. The cascade was built inside this company; the framework is what travels, not a claim that every brand in these towers ran an Olay-quality choice process.
blocks.credit: Derek Jensen (Tysto) / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0

sections.title: Prestige science beauty in Japan while Olay chose mass

blocks.text: Olay’s cascade chose mass doors on purpose. In the same decades, prestige and “science beauty” were thickening in Japan and across East Asian cities — counters, serums, and clinic-like retail that never pretended to be a drugstore endcap. Shiseido’s research campus and urban towers are one visible institutional form of that bet. P&G’s own SK-II line, with deep Japan roots, lived in the prestige logic Olay’s masstige strategy explicitly did not make primary. Contemporaneous does not mean copied: different where-to-play choices can sit inside one parent company.

blocks.alt: Storefront of an SK-II shop in Kyoto with red branding.
blocks.caption: SK-II shop, Kyoto, 2016. A prestige-channel face of P&G skin care in Japan — useful as the path Olay’s mass masstige choice was not taking as its main bet, not as a second full cascade case.
blocks.credit: Kyle Taylor / Wikimedia Commons / CC BY 2.0

blocks.alt: Exterior of the Shiseido Global Innovation Center building.
blocks.caption: Shiseido Global Innovation Center. A contemporaneous Japanese beauty firm investing in research infrastructure while Western mass brands were also redrawing price and channel maps. Named for the parallel industry climate, not as a Lafley/Martin exhibit.
blocks.credit: 妖精書士 / Wikimedia Commons / CC0

blocks.text: Elsewhere in consumer goods, firms were also learning — sometimes the hard way — that overlapping a scaled rival’s exact where-to-play without a crushing how-to-win is expensive. Martin’s Citrus Hill postmortem is a U.S. juice story; supermarket private-label wars and regional snack challengers elsewhere rhyme without sharing P&G’s nouns. The cascade’s portable claim is the questions, not Cincinnati’s org chart.

sections.title: A cascade can become a slide template that chooses nothing

blocks.text: Any five-box diagram can be filled with mush. “Win with consumers” as an aspiration, “everyone who buys soap” as a where-to-play, and “be great at innovation” as a capability fail Martin’s own distinctiveness test: the opposite is stupid, so the line is not strategy. The Olay story works in teaching because the exclusions are audible — not prestige doors as primary, not the overcrowded 50-plus wrinkle fight as the center, not $3.99 as the brand’s future.

Nested cascades create politics. Martin’s Motley Fool interview insists every level — corporate, Beauty, Skin Care, Olay, even a country selling team — must make choices. That is empowering in theory and conflicting in practice when a corporate where-to-play starves a brand’s how-to-win. The framework names the tension; it does not dissolve incentive systems.

Public numbers disagree in the details. Treat Martin’s Medium $2.5 billion and Motley Fool “almost $3 billion,” or 25–49 versus 35–50, as the same speaker’s retellings across years, not as a license to invent a blended “about $2.7 billion among women 30–50.” Strategy teaching that needs fake precision has already left the sources.

Overlap with earlier Saturday capsules is real and partial. Blue Ocean Strategy rebuilds a value curve and hunts noncustomers; Playing to Win insists on an integrated choice system and on saying no. Jobs to Be Done asks what progress a buyer hires; the cascade asks where the firm will play and how it will win. You can use more than one. You should not paste Cirque, a milkshake interview, or a David-and-Goliath underdog story into this lesson as if they were Olay’s $18.99 test.

sections.title: Practitioner Insights, an expanded edition, and a vocabulary that stuck

blocks.text: After 2013, Martin kept publishing Playing to Win / Practitioner Insights essays that restate the cascade for operators — including the 2021 communication piece and the KPI essay that ties trial rates to what would have to be true for masstige to work. HBR Press later issued expanded editions of the book; the five questions remained the spine. Consultancies and strategy blogs adopted “where to play / how to win” as everyday nouns, sometimes without the hard exclusions the Olay case depended on.

Lafley returned to P&G’s leadership in a later chapter of company history; that sequel is not this lesson. The portable artifact is the cascade plus the 2012 testing discipline: possibilities first, load-bearing conditions next, analysis in service of a choice you are willing to resource — and to explain on one page.

sections.title: What are you still calling “strategy” because saying no would hurt?

blocks.text: If you stripped your current strategy deck to the five cascade lines, which line still names a field or an advantage you are not actually funding — and which exclusion would make the rest of the page true?
